map.reading:
The single most important finding is not a new audience: it is that the supplied capability ledger appears to be stale on its openness claims. Public reporting and Cal.com's own blog date a move of the commercial codebase to closed source to 14 April 2026, with an MIT-licensed community edition (cal.diy) positioned for hobbyists, following a January 2026 vulnerability chain reported to permit complete account takeover and exposure of booking data including healthcare appointments. The ledger still asserts open-source, AGPL and self-hosted deployment as live capabilities (E2, E3, E15, E55, E56, E106). Any copy built on those claims should be re-verified before it is sent, and two of the existing segments lean on them.

The best-evidenced new demand is clinical. In Calendly's own public community a clinician asks for a BAA, is told there is none and no timeline, and concludes that names and email alone make the tool unusable with clients. Cal.com publishes a direct answer — a BAA on any plan at $300/month, free on Organizations and Enterprise, explicitly including solo providers. That is a blocked workflow with a named, priced remedy, and the practices are individually findable by their public consultation-booking pages. The $300 add-on is also the obvious objection for a two-person practice.

The second new candidate is a purchasing constraint rather than a feature gap: a third-party comparison puts the dedicated inbound-routing category's entry at $15,000 a year with fifteen bundled seats, which is $250 per person per month for a five-person revenue team. Teams below that floor still have the problem. The counterevidence in the same source — that generalist schedulers have shallower CRM routing than purpose-built routers — is the likeliest reason an evaluation fails, and should be conceded rather than argued.

The three retained segments are unchanged in definition and kept under their exact existing names. The dev-tool founder segment now carries real counterevidence: the openness that its named testimonials trade on has been withdrawn, and technical founders are publicly cancelling. The regulated-ops segment gains a hard external proof (the incumbent will not sign a BAA) and a hard external problem (the disclosed takeover chain) at the same time. The small-practice routing segment remains the weakest evidenced — the workflow failure is described by competing vendors rather than by buyers, and the supplied ledger still contradicts itself on whether routing forms are a free or Teams entitlement.

The last two candidates are flagged exploratory on purpose. Self-hosters facing the licence change are a dated, findable, forced decision, but every buyer voice found was leaving rather than upgrading, so this may be an exit population. The automation-agency channel rests on a single published account, and its concrete detail is a migration ticket.
map.note: Coverage gaps and failed searches. Reddit and other first-person forum sources did not surface for any query; the buyer voices obtained are from Hacker News, Calendly's own community forum and one agency blog, so first-person evidence is thinner than the segment list implies. A search for university and academic-advising scheduling complaints returned only vendor marketing and produced no buyer voice — no education segment is proposed. A German-language search on GDPR and Auftragsverarbeitung showed a live DACH market for EU-hosted and self-hosted scheduling, but every result was a competitor's comparison page rather than a buyer, and Cal.com's answer there was self-hosting, which the April 2026 change undermines — so no DACH segment is proposed either, despite plausible demand. Recruiting and interview-scheduling teams showed a specific limit (round-robin that does not balance interviewer load across a multi-round loop) but only through vendor round-ups; not proposed for the same reason. No search was run on geography, language or exclusions because the scope left them unspecified. Population counts are unknown throughout; fit is zero and assessment left for separate validation. Two supplied-ledger contradictions were not resolvable from public sources and remain live risks for copy: Teams at $12/user/month versus $15/member, and 'Mobile App' on the pricing page versus help docs stating no mobile app exists.

dossier.orientation: For a small consulting team, Cal.com is the booking layer behind a discovery-call page: it holds the event types, the intake/routing form that decides which consultant a given inquiry lands with, and the calendar availability those.

ranked_relevance.why: Directly names deliberate assignment by expertise, language, location or availability, which is the exact replacement for the random round-robin handoff this audience complains about.
Attribute-based routing on the prospect's own answers (industry, challenge, language) is the mechanism by which a call reaches a consultant with the right skill set.
Round-robin distribution governed by weights and priority rules speaks to the researched complaint about distribution being random rather than deliberate.
Routing forms that question the visitor and send them to the closest-matching bookable event match the intake-then-route flow already published on these firms' discovery pages.
Intake forms that collect qualifying information before booking are what give the receiving consultant context instead of a cold handoff.
Booking types plus routing logic per format covers the individual discovery call and the group session on the same team page.
Second, independently sourced statement of the routing-form behaviour, useful as corroboration rather than a separate fact.
A no-code builder matters because a small firm changes its service lines and consultant roster without engineering help.
States the plan on which routing forms are listed, which the buyer needs in order to price the routing capability.
Routing by custom variables is the deeper form of the same capability and names the tier it sits on.
Host approval before a booking is finalized mirrors the researched behaviour of reviewing an inquiry before a scheduling link is honoured.
Opt-in events are the product form of the two-path discovery page these firms already run.
Booking limits including buffer, duration and frequency are the only ledger material bearing on a consultant having open time around a call.
Controlling how far in advance a call can be booked is the closest licensed lever on the four-hours-notice prep complaint.
Buffer time is a concrete, small mechanism for not landing back-to-back discovery calls.
This audience is named as running a team Calendly, so one-click import of Calendly events addresses the switching cost that stands in front of everything else.
A multi-stage intake-to-confirmation journey is the shape of the discovery flow already documented on these sites.
CRM sync of client data and scheduling activity gives the receiving consultant the record before the call.
Two-way Salesforce and HubSpot sync is relevant only if the firm runs one of those CRMs, which the research does not establish.
Routing by account ownership is a sales-team framing of routing, adjacent to but not the same as routing by consultant expertise.
The Teams price is the number a small firm needs to evaluate team routing, but it is not itself a reason to care.
A 14-day trial lowers the cost of testing a routing change against a live inbound funnel.
The free tier's stated inclusion of routing forms and workflows sets the floor for what this audience can try without spending.
Free individual accounts frame the entry point, though a routing team is the actual unit of purchase here.
A named founder stating he migrated from Calendly is the nearest proof of the exact switch this audience would be making.
A direct comparison to Calendly and SavvyCal is orienting, but it is an aesthetic judgment with no bearing on routing outcomes.
Calendar coverage across Google, Outlook and Apple matters because a small consulting team's consultants rarely share one provider.
Booking analytics could eventually show whether routing changed who takes which call, but no evidence ties it to that use.
True and licensed, but the research surfaced no compliance requirement for this segment, so certifications would displace the routing point.
HIPAA and EU-US DPF are credible but off-topic for a consulting firm whose researched pain is call assignment.

problem_fits.caveat: The ledger covers the assignment half of the problem (attribute- and expertise-based routing, weighted round-robin, intake forms) but only indirectly touches the preparation half: the strongest material on prep is generic booking limits.
problem_fits.why: Cal.com has verified, specific product material for routing a client to the right consultant by expertise, language and availability rather than at random, which is exactly the deliberate-assignment the GitLab-sourced complaint asks for.

segment_objections.objection: We already run a team Calendly round robin on our discovery page; moving it risks breaking a funnel that at least produces booked calls.
segment_objections.answer: Cal.com imports Calendly events in one click, a named founder states he migrated from Calendly, and the Teams tier can be trialled for 14 days before the live page is switched over.

segment_objections.objection: Routing that is smart enough to pick the right consultant is probably an enterprise feature we cannot justify for a handful of people.
segment_objections.answer: Routing forms are listed as part of the free account's feature set and the Teams tier that formally includes routing forms and round-robin is $12 per user/month billed yearly with a 14-day trial.

segment_objections.objection: Even if the call reaches the right consultant, they still get it with no time to prepare.
segment_objections.answer: The licensed levers here are indirect: booking limits covering buffer, duration and frequency, a setting for how far in advance a call can be booked, buffer time between meetings, and opt-in events where the host approves the request.

segment_objections.objection: Our process is to read an inquiry first and only then send a scheduling link; a self-serve booking page would take that control away.
segment_objections.answer: Opt-in events require host confirmation before a booking is final and notify the host on each request, and events can be hidden or issued as single-use private links so a slot is only bookable once the firm sends it.

segment_objections.objection: Has routing like this actually worked for a consulting firm with senior people taking the discovery calls, not a software company?
Our consultants are each on different calendars and different tools; shared availability will be wrong and we will double-book a client.
segment_objections.answer: Cal.com cross-references connected calendars to derive availability, syncs Google, Outlook, Apple and Zoho in real time, places no cap on calendar connections, and only offers slots where all parties are mutually free — with the caveat.
